card.name: Raibenshe
card.tagline: A fierce martial folk dance from Bengal executed with long bamboo poles.
card.profile: Raibenshe is a traditional Bengali folk martial dance performed exclusively by men. Originating from the Bagdi community who served as bodyguards to medieval landlords in Bengal, the genre takes its name from the raibansh, a long bamboo stick used during performance. Dancers enact combat gestures including drawing bows, throwing spears, and waving swords to the accompaniment of dhol drums and kanshi cymbals. Today, it is primarily performed in the Birbhum, Bardhaman, and Murshidabad districts of West Bengal.
card.insight: Originating among medieval Bengal's landlord bodyguards, Raibenshe dancers wear brass anklets only on their right ankle while executing martial acrobatics with bamboo sticks.

card.profile_long:
Raibenshe is a traditional genre of Bengali folk martial dance executed exclusively by male performers. Historically, this martial dance form was performed by members of the Bagdi community. In medieval Bengal, the Bagdi community frequently served as armed bodyguards to local landlords (zamindars), developing martial disciplines that eventually evolved into the Raibenshe dance tradition.

The dance derives its name from the raibansh, a long bamboo stick that serves as the central prop and instrument of acrobatic expression during the performance. Performers display vigorous, highly physical movements combined with acrobatic routines utilizing these bamboo poles. Throughout the dance, the performers physically mimic battle manoeuvres, visually enacting the actions of drawing a bow, throwing a spear, and waving a sword.

The music accompanying Raibenshe relies on dynamic folk percussion to drive its martial tempo. The ensemble features the dhol, a double-headed drum, alongside kanshis, which are brass cymbals. Dancers wear a single brass anklet, known as a nupur, on their right ankle, creating a distinct percussive sound that accents their footwork against the rhythmic beat of the dhol and kanshi.

While Raibenshe was once widely popular across West Bengal, its present-day performances are mostly concentrated within specific regions. Today, the tradition is actively preserved and performed primarily in the Birbhum, Bardhaman, and Murshidabad districts of West Bengal, India.

sections.origins_and_history: Raibenshe was historically practiced by the Bagdi community in medieval Bengal, who served as bodyguards to regional landlords. The dance takes its name from the raibansh, a long bamboo stick used in martial displays.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance features vigorous and manly body movements accompanied by acrobatics using long bamboo sticks. Male dancers enact martial actions such as drawing a bow, throwing a spear, and waving a sword. A single brass anklet (nupur) is worn on the right ankle to accent movement.
sections.music_and_instruments: Performances are accompanied musically by dhols (traditional double-headed drums) and kanshis (cymbals). The sound is further accented by the nupur brass anklet on the dancer's right foot.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear a brass anklet called a nupur exclusively on their right ankle. The dance involves the physical prop of the raibansh, a long bamboo pole.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally linked to the martial duties and bodyguard traditions of the Bagdi community in medieval Bengal, the dance embodies martial prowess and athletic skill.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is performed primarily across the Birbhum, Bardhaman, and Murshidabad districts of West Bengal, India.
sections.lineage: Originating within the Bagdi community of medieval Bengal, Raibenshe sits within the broader spectrum of Indian folk and Bengali martial dances.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Martial Bamboo Dancers of Bengal
episode_brief.logline: Discover how the medieval bodyguards of Bengal transformed combat training with long bamboo sticks into a high-energy acrobatic folk dance.
beats: Introduce the historical roots of Raibenshe among the Bagdi bodyguards in medieval Bengal.
Demonstrate the raibansh bamboo pole and the percussive nupur worn on the right ankle.
Show musicians driving the energy with dhol drums and kanshi cymbals.
Detail the martial pantomime gestures: drawing the bow, throwing the spear, and waving the sword.
Highlight acrobatic maneuvers performed with the bamboo poles in Birbhum.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the primary martial gestures and posture.
drills: Practice the bow-drawing arm extension in a wide stance.

visual_motifs: Long bamboo poles (raibansh) swinging in dynamic arcs.
Close-up of the brass anklet (nupur) on the right ankle striking the ground.
Traditional dhol and kanshi musicians playing rapidly.
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An energetic martial artist and cultural historian passionate about preserving ancient South Asian physical traditions.
episode_brief.music_cue: Upbeat, driving dhol drumming accompanied by sharp kanshi cymbal strikes.

seniors.seated_version: Perform the martial upper-body mime gestures—drawing a bow, throwing a spear, and waving a sword—from a seated position without acrobatic bamboo maneuvers.
seniors.standing_version: Execute gentle upper-body martial gestures while standing, omitting jump acrobatics and pole balancing.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Perform at a moderate tempo with reduced arm extension range.
seniors.counts: 4-count arms for bow drawing, 4-count arms for spear throwing.
avoid: Heavy twisting or pole manipulation that risks loss of balance

children.game_version: A martial reaction game where children mime bow, spear, and sword actions on command using light foam or short light sticks.
